commentary.bottom_line: Seventeen sources endorse documenting bias assessment methods, subgroup performance, underrepresented populations, and residual bias in model cards, but no supplied study tests whether this documentation changes how users apply AI or reduces harm to patients in low-accuracy groups. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and draft regulatory guidance, and no study was supplied that documents the hazard itself.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests the practice, and none documents how often users are unaware of low-accuracy populations. The endorsements come from frameworks, draft guidance, and commentaries. Under GRADE conventions this gives no direct evidence, so any benefit from model-card bias reporting is assumed rather than measured.

A model card can only prevent harm if a clinician reads it and changes a decision for a patient in an affected subgroup. No supplied study measures whether disclosure changes user behavior at the point of care. The safeguard's ability to intercept errors before they reach patients therefore remains untested.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks sponsors to explain missing demographic data and how the resulting risks are controlled. CHAI, NIST AI 600-1, and FUTURE-AI make similar documentation recommendations. These sources set expectations for disclosure. They do not provide outcome data showing that disclosure works.

Several commentaries propose subgroup reporting and calibration by sex, ethnicity, and age as a check on inequitable performance. No supplied study reports subgroup results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. It is also unknown whether documentation leads deployers to act on gaps affecting these groups.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployments with and without subgroup performance and residual-bias disclosures. These studies should measure whether clinicians read the disclosures, whether they adjust their reliance on AI output for affected subgroups, and whether error rates or patient outcomes differ in those subgroups. Baseline studies that measure how often users are unaware of low-accuracy populations would also establish the size of the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Health systems serving these patients have no evidence that model-card disclosures identify or reduce performance gaps affecting them. They may need to run their own local subgroup evaluations rather than rely on developer documentation.
